chapters.title: מַלְכַּת עַכְבְּרֵי הַשָּׂדֶה
chapters.orig_title: The Queen of the Field Mice

w: לֹא יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת שֶׁ|it can't be that|~idiom
s.line: “We cannot be far from the road of yellow brick, now,” remarked the Scarecrow, as he stood beside the girl,
s.note: לֹא יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת שֶׁ… = "it can't be that …", a very common way to say that something is impossible or unbelievable. On its own, לֹא יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת! = "No way! That can't be!"

s.line: “for we have come nearly as far as the river carried us away.”
s.note: סָחַף = to sweep away (of water or wind). Its nif'al נִסְחַף = "got swept away", also used for people: נִסְחַפְתִּי = "I got carried away". סַחַף is soil erosion.

w: עָמַד לַעֲנוֹת|was about to answer|~idiom: עָמַד לְ־ = was about to
s.line: The Tin Woodman was about to reply when he heard a low growl,
s.note: עָמַד לְ־ + infinitive = "was about to": הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס עוֹמֵד לָצֵאת (the bus is about to leave). The verb keeps its form (עוֹמֵד, עָמַד) but has nothing to do with standing here.

s.line: and turning his head (which worked beautifully on hinges) he saw a strange beast come bounding over the grass toward them.
s.note: One root, two binyanim: סוֹבֵב = to turn something (he turned his head), and הִסְתּוֹבֵב (hitpa'el) = to turn by itself (the head turned). הִסְתּוֹבֵב also means "to wander around": הִסְתּוֹבַבְנוּ בָּעִיר. In hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first root letter ס.

w: חֲתוּל בָּר|a wildcat|~lit. cat of the wild
s.line: It was, indeed, a great yellow Wildcat,
and the Woodman thought it must be chasing something, for its ears were lying close to its head and its mouth was wide open,
s.note: רָדַף אַחֲרֵי = to chase (literally "to pursue after"). רְדִיפָה is a chase, and also persecution. פָּתוּחַ לִרְוָחָה = wide open, a fixed phrase used of doors, windows and mouths.

s.line: showing two rows of ugly teeth, while its red eyes glowed like balls of fire.
As it came nearer the Tin Woodman saw that running before the beast was a little gray field mouse,
s.note: עַכְבַּר שָׂדֶה is a construct pair ("mouse of field"), so the first word shortens its vowel: עַכְבָּר → עַכְבַּר. In the plural, עַכְבָּרִים → עַכְבְּרֵי הַשָּׂדֶה, as in this chapter's title. Note that the article goes on the second word only.

w: הָיָה לוֹ|he had|~lit. there was to him
לֹא בְּסֵדֶר|is wrong|~lit. not in order
s.line: and although he had no heart he knew it was wrong for the Wildcat to try to kill such a pretty, harmless creature.
s.note: לֹא בְּסֵדֶר ("not in order") is the everyday way to say "wrong, not OK": זֶה לֹא בְּסֵדֶר מִמְּךָ = "that's not fair of you". מַזִּיק (hif'il) = harmful; נֵזֶק = damage. חָמוּד = cute, the word you'll hear for babies and puppies.

s.line: So the Woodman raised his axe,

w: חָלַף עַל פָּנָיו|passed by him|~idiom: lit. passed over his face
s.line: and as the Wildcat ran by he gave it a quick blow that cut the beast’s head clean off from its body,
s.note: הִנְחִית מַכָּה = to land a blow, a set phrase. הִנְחִית (hif'il of נ־ח־ת) means "to bring down, to land"; a pilot מַנְחִית a plane, and נְחִיתָה is a landing. חָלַף עַל פָּנָיו = "passed right by him".

s.line: and it rolled over at his feet in two pieces.
The field mouse, now that it was freed from its enemy, stopped short;
s.note: שֻׁחְרַר is pu'al, the passive of שִׁחְרֵר (to set free, to release), from a four-letter root. Both are news words: הָאָסִיר שֻׁחְרַר = the prisoner was released; a soldier finishing army service is מְשֻׁחְרָר. בְּבַת אַחַת = all at once, suddenly.

s.line: and coming slowly up to the Woodman it said, in a squeaky little voice:
s.note: מְצַפְצֵף = squeaking or chirping. A car horn also מְצַפְצֵף, and צְפִירָה is a siren. Slang: אֲנִי מְצַפְצֵף עַל זֶה = "I don't give a hoot about it".

s.line: “Oh, thank you!
Thank you ever so much for saving my life.”
s.note: "Thank you for …": תּוֹדָה עַל + noun (תּוֹדָה עַל הָעֶזְרָה), but תּוֹדָה עַל שֶׁ… + a verb in the past (תּוֹדָה עַל שֶׁבָּאתָ). חַיִּים (life) is always plural: הַחַיִּים שֶׁלִּי.

s.line: “Don’t speak of it, I beg of you,” replied the Woodman.
s.note: אֵין צֹרֶךְ = "there's no need" (+ infinitive). הוֹדָה (hif'il) has two meanings: "to thank" (הוֹדָה לְ־ someone) and "to admit, confess" (הוֹדָה בְּ־ something). תּוֹדָה comes from the same root.

w: אֵין לִי|I don't have|~lit. there isn't to me
s.line: “I have no heart, you know,
so I am careful to help all those who may need a friend,
s.note: הִקְפִּיד = to be careful to do something, to make a point of it: הוּא מַקְפִּיד לָבוֹא בַּזְּמַן (he always makes sure to be on time). With עַל: הִקְפִּיד עַל = to insist on, be strict about.

s.line: even if it happens to be only a mouse.”
“Only a mouse!” cried the little animal, indignantly.
s.note: בְּהִתְרַעֲמוּת = with indignation, a higher-register word (from the hitpa'el הִתְרַעֵם, to resent, to complain angrily). In everyday speech you'd say בְּכַעַס. Note that חַיָּה is feminine, so קָרְאָה.

s.line: “Why, I am a Queen—the Queen of all the Field Mice!”
s.note: הֲרֵי = "why, after all, but surely": it presents something the speaker thinks is obvious. הֲרֵי אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ! = "But I told you!"

s.line: “Oh, indeed,” said the Woodman, making a bow.
“Therefore you have done a great deed, as well as a brave one, in saving my life,” added the Queen.
s.note: עָשָׂה מַעֲשֶׂה: verb and noun from the same root, as in קָד קִידָה. הוֹסִיף (hif'il) = to add, and in dialogue "to add, go on to say". The Queen is feminine: הוֹסִיפָה.

s.line: At that moment several mice were seen running up as fast as their little legs could carry them,
s.note: You know נִרְאָה as "looks, seems". Here it has its other, passive meaning: נִרְאוּ = "were seen", the nif'al of רָאָה (to see). כְּכָל שֶׁ… = "as much as": מַהֵר כְּכָל שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר = as fast as possible.

s.line: and when they saw their Queen they exclaimed:

w: הוֹד מַלְכוּתֵךְ|your Majesty (fem.)|~lit. the splendor of your kingship
שֶׁתֵּהָרְגִי|that you would be killed|!nif'al · ה־ר־ג
s.line: “Oh, your Majesty, we thought you would be killed!
s.note: תֵּהָרְגִי is the future of the nif'al נֶהֱרַג = was killed, the passive of הָרַג. You'll meet נֶהֱרַג constantly in news reports. הוֹד מַלְכוּתֵךְ: the ending ךְ with a tsere marks "your" for a woman; to a king it is הוֹד מַלְכוּתְךָ.

s.line: How did you manage to escape the great Wildcat?”
s.note: הִצְלִיחַ + infinitive = "to manage to, succeed in". נִמְלַט = to escape, flee, a slightly formal word you'll see in the news: הַחָשׁוּד נִמְלַט (the suspect fled). Everyday speech uses בָּרַח.

s.line: They all bowed so low to the little Queen that they almost stood upon their heads.
“This funny tin man,” she answered, “killed the Wildcat and saved my life.
s.note: מַצְחִיק = funny, literally "making (someone) laugh": the hif'il participle of צָחַק (to laugh). The hif'il often means "to cause": צָחַק laughed → הִצְחִיק made laugh.

s.line: So hereafter you must all serve him, and obey his slightest wish.”
s.note: מִלֵּא (pi'el) = to fill, and with a wish, request or task, "to fulfill, carry out": מִלֵּא אֶת הַבַּקָּשָׁה, מִלֵּא טֹפֶס (filled in a form). לְשָׁרֵת = to serve; שֵׁרוּת צְבָאִי = military service.

s.line: “We will!” cried all the mice, in a shrill chorus.
And then they scampered in all directions, for Toto had awakened from his sleep,
s.note: הִתְפַּזֵּר (hitpa'el) = to scatter, disperse. The police tell a crowd לְהִתְפַּזֵּר; and מְפֻזָּר (pu'al) describes a scatterbrained person. Hebrew has no past perfect: הִתְעוֹרֵר covers "had awakened".

s.line: and seeing all these mice around him he gave one bark of delight and jumped right into the middle of the group.
Toto had always loved to chase mice when he lived in Kansas, and he saw no harm in it.
s.note: לֹא רָאָה בָּזֶה שׁוּם פְּסוּל = "saw nothing wrong with it", a set phrase in a slightly higher register. פָּסוּל (pa'ul) = disqualified, unfit: a ballot or a goal can be פָּסוּל.

s.line: But the Tin Woodman caught the dog in his arms and held him tight, while he called to the mice,
s.note: הֶחֱזִיק (hif'il) = to hold, and חָזָק = strong, tight: same root ח־ז־ק. תַּחֲזִיק מַעֲמָד! = "Hang in there!"

s.line: “Come back! Come back! Toto shall not hurt you.”
s.note: תַּחְזְרוּ is the future form used as a command, which is how people usually give orders in spoken Hebrew (the true imperative is חִזְרוּ). פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hurt, hit, harm; נִפְגַּע = was hurt, injured.

s.line: At this the Queen of the Mice stuck her head out from underneath a clump of grass and asked, in a timid voice,
s.note: לְשֵׁמַע + noun = "on hearing": לְשֵׁמַע הַחֲדָשׁוֹת (on hearing the news). הוֹצִיא (hif'il of יָצָא, to go out) = to take out, make something go out; it is also "to spend" money: הוֹצֵאוֹת = expenses.

s.line: “Are you sure he will not bite us?”
“I will not let him,” said the Woodman;
“so do not be afraid.”
s.note: A negative command is אַל + the future: אַל תְּפַחֵד (to a man), אַל תְּפַחֲדִי (to a woman), אַל תְּפַחֲדוּ (to a group). Never לֹא with the imperative. הִרְשָׁה = to allow; רְשׁוּת = permission, also "authority" (רְשׁוּת הַמִּסִּים, the Tax Authority).

s.line: One by one the mice came creeping back,
and Toto did not bark again, although he tried to get out of the Woodman’s arms,
s.note: הִשְׁתַּחְרֵר is the hitpa'el of the root you met above in שֻׁחְרַר: "to free oneself, break loose", and also "to relax, loosen up": תִּשְׁתַּחְרֵר! = "Loosen up!" As in הִסְתּוֹבֵב, the ת swaps places with the first root letter שׁ. אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although, a little more formal than לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ.

w: הָיָה נוֹשֵׁךְ|would have bitten|~conditional: הָיָה + participle
הָיָה יוֹדֵעַ|he had known|~conditional: הָיָה + participle
s.line: and would have bitten him had he not known very well he was made of tin.
s.note: Unreal conditions ("would have …, if he had …") use הָיָה + participle in both halves: אִם הָיִיתִי יוֹדֵעַ, הָיִיתִי בָּא = "If I had known, I would have come." עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of.

s.line: Finally one of the biggest mice spoke.
“Is there anything we can do,” it asked, “to repay you for saving the life of our Queen?”
s.note: גָּמַל לְ־ = to repay someone (for good or ill); גְּמוּל = reward, recompense. Without vowels גמל is also גָּמָל, a camel, and גְּמִילָה means weaning, or kicking a habit: גְּמִילָה מֵעִשּׁוּן = quitting smoking.

w: לֹא שֶׁאֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ|not that I know of|~idiom
s.line: “Nothing that I know of,” answered the Woodman;
s.note: לֹא שֶׁאֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ = "not that I know of", used exactly like the English. יֵשׁ פֹּה מִישֶׁהוּ? – לֹא שֶׁאֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ.

s.line: but the Scarecrow, who had been trying to think, but could not because his head was stuffed with straw, said, quickly,
s.note: מְמֻלָּא is the pu'al participle of מִלֵּא (to fill), which you met a few sentences back: pi'el מִלֵּא filled → pu'al מְמֻלָּא filled, stuffed. In the kitchen, מְמֻלָּאִים are stuffed vegetables.

s.line: “Oh, yes; you can save our friend, the Cowardly Lion, who is asleep in the poppy bed.”
“A Lion!” cried the little Queen.
“Why, he would eat us all up.”
s.note: טָרַף = to devour, used of predators; a beast of prey is a טוֹרֵף. It is also "to shuffle" cards. Related: טְרֵפָה (non-kosher meat, originally an animal torn by a beast).

s.line: “Oh, no,” declared the Scarecrow;
s.note: הִכְרִיז (hif'il) = to declare, announce, a common news verb: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל…. The noun is הַכְרָזָה, and כָּרוֹז is a herald, or a printed public notice.

s.line: “this Lion is a coward.”
“Really?” asked the Mouse.
s.note: עַכְבָּרָה is the feminine of עַכְבָּר. Baum calls the mouse "it", but Hebrew must pick a gender, so once we know she is a queen, the mouse becomes עַכְבָּרָה and the verb שָׁאֲלָה.

s.line: “He says so himself,” answered the Scarecrow,
“and he would never hurt anyone who is our friend.

w: בְּטוּב לֵב|kindly|~lit. with goodness of heart
s.line: If you will help us to save him I promise that he shall treat you all with kindness.”
s.note: After אִם about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense: אִם תַּעַזְרוּ = "if you help". הִבְטִיחַ (hif'il) = to promise; the same root gives בָּטוּחַ (sure, safe) and בִּטָּחוֹן (security). הִתְנַהֵג אֶל = to treat, behave toward; הִתְנַהֲגוּת = behavior.

s.line: “Very well,” said the Queen, “we trust you.
s.note: סָמַךְ עַל = to rely on, trust: אֲנִי סוֹמֵךְ עָלֶיךָ = "I'm counting on you". The same root gives סָמוּךְ (near, adjacent) and מִסְמָךְ (a document).

s.line: But what shall we do?”
s.note: עָלַי / עָלֶיךָ / עָלֵינוּ + infinitive = "I / you / we must", literally "it is on me". It is a bit more formal than אֲנַחְנוּ צְרִיכִים.

w: שֶׁקּוֹרְאִים לָךְ|who call you|pa'al ptc · ק־ר־א
s.line: “Are there many of these mice which call you Queen and are willing to obey you?”
s.note: מוּכָן = ready, willing. In form it is a hof'al participle ("made ready"), the passive of הֵכִין (to prepare). אַתָּה מוּכָן? = "Are you ready?" צִיֵּת לְ־ = to obey; צַיְּתָן = an obedient person.

s.line: “Oh, yes; there are thousands,” she replied.

w: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as soon as possible|~idiom
s.line: “Then send for them all to come here as soon as possible,
s.note: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר = as fast as possible, ASAP, the everyday phrase. The pattern כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר + adjective/adverb works widely: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר זוֹל = as cheap as possible. אִם כָּךְ = "if so, in that case".

s.line: and let each one bring a long piece of string.”
s.note: שֶׁ + future = "let …": שֶׁיָּבוֹא = "let him come". Note that אֲרֻכָּה agrees with חֲתִיכָה (feminine), not with חוּט: in a construct pair the adjective goes with the first noun.

s.line: The Queen turned to the mice that attended her and told them to go at once and get all her people.
s.note: פָּנָה אֶל = to turn to, and also to address, apply to: פָּנִיתִי לַמִּשְׂרָד (I contacted the office); פְּנִיָּה = an inquiry, and also a turn in the road. לִוָּה (pi'el) = to accompany; מְלַוֶּה = an escort.

s.line: As soon as they heard her orders they ran away in every direction as fast as possible.
s.note: בָּרֶגַע שֶׁ ("at the moment that") = as soon as: תִּתְקַשֵּׁר בָּרֶגַע שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ. כְּכָל הָאֶפְשָׁר is the more formal twin of כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר.

s.line: “Now,” said the Scarecrow to the Tin Woodman, “you must go to those trees by the riverside and make a truck that will carry the Lion.”
s.note: גְּדַת הַנָּהָר: גָּדָה (bank) becomes גְּדַת in the construct, like מַלְכָּה → מַלְכַּת. In the news, הַגָּדָה הַמַּעֲרָבִית is the West Bank (of the Jordan). Baum's "truck" is an old word for a low cart on wheels: עֲגָלָה.

s.line: So the Woodman went at once to the trees and began to work;
and he soon made a truck out of the limbs of trees, from which he chopped away all the leaves and branches.
s.note: קִצֵּץ (pi'el) = to chop, trim, cut back. In the news it means cutting budgets: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה קִצְּצָה בַּתַּקְצִיב, and קִצּוּצִים are spending cuts. In a recipe, בָּצָל קָצוּץ = chopped onion.

s.line: He fastened it together with wooden pegs and made the four wheels out of short pieces of a big tree trunk.
s.note: אַרְבַּעַת הַגַּלְגַּלִּים = "the four wheels": to say "the two / three / four …" Hebrew puts the number in the construct form before the noun with the article: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַיְּלָדִים, שְׁתֵּי הַבָּנוֹת. חִבֵּר (pi'el) = to join, connect, and also to add up numbers (חִבּוּר = addition).

s.line: So fast and so well did he work that by the time the mice began to arrive the truck was all ready for them.
They came from all directions, and there were thousands of them: big mice and little mice and middle-sized mice;
s.note: בֵּינוֹנִי = medium, average, from בֵּין (between). It also means "mediocre": הַסֶּרֶט הָיָה בֵּינוֹנִי. In grammar, בֵּינוֹנִי is the Hebrew name for the present-tense participle.

s.line: and each one brought a piece of string in his mouth.
It was about this time that Dorothy woke from her long sleep and opened her eyes.
s.note: פָּקַח is used only for opening the eyes (the opposite of עָצַם). From the same root: פִּקֵּחַ = clever, sharp (literally "open-eyed") and פַּקָּח = an inspector, the one who gives you a parking ticket.

s.line: She was greatly astonished to find herself lying upon the grass, with thousands of mice standing around and looking at her timidly.
s.note: הִתְפַּלֵּא (hitpa'el) = to be amazed, to wonder; פֶּלֶא = a wonder, and אֵין פֶּלֶא שֶׁ… = "no wonder that …". הִבִּיט בְּ־ = to look at: the verb takes בְּ. After "found that" Hebrew keeps the present tense (שׁוֹכֶבֶת).

s.line: But the Scarecrow told her about everything, and turning to the dignified little Mouse, he said:
s.note: מְכֻבָּד (pu'al participle of כִּבֵּד, to honor) = honored, respected, dignified. אוֹרֵחַ מְכֻבָּד = a guest of honor. The pi'el כִּבֵּד also means "to offer food": תִּתְכַּבְּדוּ! = "Help yourselves!"

s.line: “Permit me to introduce to you her Majesty, the Queen.”
s.note: הַרְשִׁי לִי is the true imperative of הִרְשָׁה (to allow), polite and a little formal; in speech you'd hear תַּרְשִׁי לִי. הִצִּיג = to introduce, present, and also to perform: הַצָּגָה = a play, a show. הִצִּיג בִּפְנֵי = to present to someone.

w: הֵנִיעָה בְּרֹאשָׁהּ|nodded|~idiom: lit. moved with her head
s.line: Dorothy nodded gravely and the Queen made a curtsy,
s.note: הֵנִיעַ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ = to nod (hif'il of נ־ו־ע, to move). Related: מָנוֹעַ = an engine, and תְּנוּעָה = movement, also traffic, or a political movement. בִּרְצִינוּת = seriously; בִּרְצִינוּת? = "Seriously?"

s.line: after which she became quite friendly with the little girl.
s.note: הִתְיַדֵּד עִם (hitpa'el) = to make friends with, from יָדִיד (friend). The hitpa'el often means "to become": הִתְיַדֵּד became friendly, הִתְעַיֵּף got tired, הִתְבַּגֵּר grew up.

s.line: The Scarecrow and the Woodman now began to fasten the mice to the truck, using the strings they had brought.
s.note: בְּעֶזְרַת = "with the help of, by means of" (construct of עֶזְרָה). It is the natural way to translate "using": פָּתַחְתִּי אֶת זֶה בְּעֶזְרַת סַכִּין. Religious speakers say בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם, "God willing".

s.line: One end of a string was tied around the neck of each mouse and the other end to the truck.
s.note: Three forms of one root: קָשַׁר (pa'al) tied, נִקְשַׁר (nif'al) was tied, and the pa'ul קָשׁוּר = tied. נִקְשַׁר also means "became attached to" someone, and קָשׁוּר לְ־ = connected, related to: זֶה לֹא קָשׁוּר = "that's beside the point".

w: פִּי אֶלֶף|a thousand times|~idiom: פִּי = times
s.line: Of course the truck was a thousand times bigger than any of the mice who were to draw it;
s.note: פִּי + number = "… times (as much)": פִּי שְׁנַיִם = twice as much, פִּי אֶלֶף = a thousand times. אָמוּר לְ־ (literally "said to") = supposed to: הוּא אָמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ בְּשֶׁבַע (he's supposed to arrive at seven).

s.line: but when all the mice had been harnessed, they were able to pull it quite easily.
s.note: נִרְתַּם = was harnessed (nif'al of רָתַם, to harness). In the news it is used figuratively with an active meaning: כֻּלָּם נִרְתְּמוּ לַמְּשִׂימָה = everyone got on board and pitched in.

s.line: Even the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman could sit on it,
and were drawn swiftly by their queer little horses to the place where the Lion lay asleep.
s.note: עַל יְדֵי = "by", naming who does the action in a passive sentence: נִמְשְׁכוּ עַל יְדֵי הַסּוּסִים. נִמְשַׁךְ also has active meanings: "to be drawn to, attracted" (הוּא נִמְשָׁךְ אֵלֶיהָ) and "to go on, last" (הַפְּגִישָׁה נִמְשְׁכָה שָׁעָה).

s.line: After a great deal of hard work, for the Lion was heavy, they managed to get him up on the truck.
s.note: הֶעֱלָה (hif'il of עָלָה, to go up) = to raise, bring up, put up. It is also "to raise" prices (הֶעֱלוּ אֶת הַמְּחִירִים) and to upload: הֶעֱלֵיתִי תְּמוּנָה.

w: לָצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ|to set out|~idiom: lit. go out to the road
s.line: Then the Queen hurriedly gave her people the order to start, for she feared if the mice stayed among the poppies too long they also would fall asleep.
s.note: מִהֵר (pi'el) + infinitive = "to hurry to do": Hebrew often turns an English adverb ("hurriedly") into a verb like this. מַהֵר, "quickly", is from the same root. לָצֵאת לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out on a journey.

s.line: At first the little creatures, many though they were, could hardly stir the heavily loaded truck;
s.note: בְּקֹשִׁי = "with difficulty", and also "barely, hardly": בְּקֹשִׁי יָשַׁנְתִּי = "I hardly slept". עָמוּס = loaded, and in everyday speech "swamped, busy": הַיּוֹם שֶׁלִּי עָמוּס; עֹמֶס = load, heavy traffic.

s.line: but the Woodman and the Scarecrow both pushed from behind, and they got along better.
s.note: הִתְקַדֵּם (hitpa'el) = to move forward, make progress; הִתְקַדְּמוּת = progress. אֵיךְ הָעִנְיָנִים? = "How are things?"

s.line: Soon they rolled the Lion out of the poppy bed to the green fields,
s.note: גִּלְגֵּל (pi'el) = to roll something; הִתְגַּלְגֵּל (hitpa'el) = to roll by itself, as the wildcat's head did at the start of the chapter. גַּלְגַּל (wheel) is from the same root.

s.line: where he could breathe the sweet, fresh air again, instead of the poisonous scent of the flowers.

w: יָצְאָה לִקְרָאתָם|came out to meet them|~idiom
s.line: Dorothy came to meet them and thanked the little mice warmly for saving her companion from death.
s.note: יָצָא לִקְרַאת = to go out to meet someone. לִקְרַאת alone means "toward, ahead of": לִקְרַאת הַחַג = in the run-up to the holiday. הוֹדָה לְ־ … עַל = to thank someone for something.

w: הִתְחַבֵּב עָלֶיהָ|had grown dear to her|hitpa'el · ח־ב־ב
s.line: She had grown so fond of the big Lion she was glad he had been rescued.
s.note: הִתְחַבֵּב עַל = to become dear to, win someone's affection: הַכֶּלֶב הִתְחַבֵּב עַל כֻּלָּם. Notice the Hebrew turns the sentence around: the Lion grew dear to her. נִצַּל (nif'al) = was saved, the passive of הִצִּיל (hif'il); נִצּוֹל is a survivor.

s.line: Then the mice were unharnessed from the truck and scampered away through the grass to their homes.
The Queen of the Mice was the last to leave.
“If ever you need us again,” she said, “come out into the field and call, and we shall hear you and come to your assistance.
s.note: נִשְׁמַע here is "we will hear" (pa'al future, אֲנַחְנוּ form). Spelled the same, נִשְׁמַע is also the nif'al "sounds, is heard": מָה נִשְׁמַע? = "How are you? What's new?" הִצְטָרֵךְ = to need (hitpa'el of צ־ר־ךְ): after a צ the ת turns into ט.

s.line: Good-bye!”
s.note: לְהִתְרָאוֹת = good-bye, literally "to see each other (again)", a hitpa'el with a reciprocal meaning, like הִתְכַּתְּבוּ (wrote to each other).

s.line: “Good-bye!” they all answered,
and away the Queen ran, while Dorothy held Toto tightly lest he should run after her and frighten her.
s.note: רָצָה is a word to watch: "she ran" (from ר־ו־ץ) and "he wanted" (from ר־צ־ה) are spelled and pointed exactly alike. Only context tells you which. הִבְהִיל = to frighten, alarm; בֶּהָלָה = panic.

s.line: After this they sat down beside the Lion until he should awaken;

w: לַאֲרוּחַת הַצָּהֳרַיִם|for lunch|~lit. for the meal of noon
s.line: and the Scarecrow brought Dorothy some fruit from a tree near by, which she ate for her dinner.
s.note: In Baum's America "dinner" was often the main meal at midday, so here it is אֲרוּחַת הַצָּהֳרַיִם, lunch, the main meal of the day in many Israeli homes too. סָמוּךְ = nearby; סָמוּךְ לְ־ = close to: סָמוּךְ לַתַּחֲנָה.
